meaning: ‘The Attacker’ — a name of Kārttikeya, son of Śiva (or of Agni), the god of war who leads the divine hosts against the enemies of the gods.

phonemes.desc: The cluster sk is preserved; short a as in “cup”.
The name means “the Attacker”, “the Leaper” — a war-name, not a birth-name.
The cluster sk is preserved in every period of the language; no sound is lost between the s and the k.

pronunciation.note: One god, six names per tradition — born of six sparks from the gods’ outraged eyes.

domains.title: God of War, the Divine Hosts
domains.subtitle: The Six-Headed General of the Gods’ Army
domains.lead: Skanda is the Hindu war-god: the ever-youthful general of the devas’ hosts, born from the combined fire of Śiva’s third eye to destroy the demon Tāraka. Tamil India knows him as Murugan, the eternally beautiful mountain lord of the six abodes; the Sanskrit world as Kārttikeya, son of the Pleiades’ fosterage.

cards.name: The Divine General
cards.desc: Commander of the gods’ armies — the deva-senāpati — before whom no asura line holds.

cards.name: Born of the Third Eye
cards.desc: Six sparks from the gods’ wrath-eyes, fostered by the Kṛttikā — the Pleiades — as six infants, fused into one.

cards.name: The Spear
cards.desc: Śakti, the lance his mother Umā gave him — one throw ended Tāraka, the boon-armed demon.

cards.name: Lord of the Six Abodes
cards.desc: Murugan’s six mountain shrines from Tirupparankunram to Palani mark his Tamil country.

mythology.lead: The Skanda myth is the war-god’s birth-saga: the gods, unable to defeat Tāraka, whose boon made him unkillable except by a son of Śiva, contrived the god’s marriage to Pārvatī; the child was born as fire from the third eye, fostered by the Pleiades, and general of heaven before he was a week old. The Tamil Murugan traditions add the wooing of Vaḷḷi, the huntress, and the gnostic doctrine of the Arupadaiveedu, the six stations of grace.

myths.title: The Birth of Fire
myths.text: When Agni and the river Ganges could not carry the god’s seed, they left it in the reeds of the Gangā’s bank; six infants were found there by the six Kṛttikā nymphs, each nursing one — until Pārvatī gathered them into a single six-headed child. His first week closed with the death of Tāraka, slain by the spear his mother gave him.

myths.title: The Deva-Senāpati
myths.text: The great Purāṇa bearing his name makes him general of the gods’ hosts and husband of Devasenā — ‘the army of the gods’ — a marriage arranged before his birth. His camp is on the world’s margin; his peacock mount, the demon Siṃhakeśin subdued, struts beneath his banner.

myths.title: Vaḷḷi and Teyvāyāṉai
myths.text: The Tamil epics tell how Murugan wooed the huntress Vaḷḷi in the guise of a tree-shade, and wed both her and Teyvāyāṉai, Indra’s daughter, in the great marriage at Tiruchendur. The legend’s two wives read theologically: divine grace (Teyvāyāṉai) and the soul’s own effort (Vaḷḷi) are both needed for union with the lord.

myths.title: The Sage-Child
myths.text: As Subrahmaṇya — ‘the dear one to the Brahmins’ — he is the teacher-god, expounding the Vedas to his own father Śiva in the role of guru. The image flips the war-god into wisdom’s child, and fixes his southern temples as places of learning as much as of arms.

lore.syncretism: Skanda is the great pan-Indian convergence: Vedic Rudra’s son, Tamil Murugan, Buddhist Kārttikeya of the north, and the Graha of the week’s Tuesday. The Greeks of the Northwest compared him to Ares and Mars; the Kushan coins show him as Skanda-Kumāra beside the Buddha. His peacock entered Christian art’s immortality symbolism by the strangest of roads.
lore.culturalLegacy: Murugan is Tamil country’s beloved god — the Kanda Ṣaṣṭhī festival at Tiruchendur draws millions, and the god’s hill-shrines anchor Tamil sacred geography. His six-headed infant image, the Kārttikeya of Gupta art, defined the war-god’s iconography for Asia; and the Ṣaṣṭhī vow is observed across the subcontinent by parents of sons.
lore.extendedMeditation: Skanda: the war-name that means ‘the one who attacks’. In plain letters it reads like what it is — a battle-cry reduced to a name. The Tamil country still shouts it in festival; the lexicon keeps it here, at rest, its spear laid across the threshold of the temple.

sources.name: Kumārasaṃbhava of Kālidāsa (the birth of the war-god)

lore.archaeology: The six abodes (Ārupadaiveṭṭu) of Tamil Nadu are his living monuments; Gupta and Kushan sculpture give him his classical six-headed infant form. The Batu Caves of Malaysia, a modern Murugan shrine of cathedral scale, extend his geography into the diaspora.
lore.cult: The Kanda Ṣaṣṭhī festival — his birth-week and the war’s anniversary — is among the largest gatherings in the Tamil world, closing with the ritual breaking of the fast. His hill-shrines are walked on foot as pilgrimage; the kavadi-bearers’ dance is his cult’s most visible modern rite.
lore.iconography: The beautiful youth, six heads arrayed as a peacock’s fan, the spear (vel) upright, riding the peacock whose spread tail is the god’s own flame; in Tamil images he stands alone with the vel, the weapon itself treated as the deity’s presence.
lore.reception: Comparative mythology pairs him with Ares, Mars, and the Chinese Erlang as the divine general; Tamil literature claims him as the grammar of Tamil devotion itself. The Batu Caves’ giant gold statue made him a global icon — the war-god who became a diaspora’s home.
